newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico think-tank sees real wages barely up in '97.
newsitem.headline: Mexico think-tank sees real wages barely up in '97.

text.p: Mexican workers can only expect a meagre real wage increase in 1997 that will still leave them worse off than before an economic crisis in December 1994, a prominent Mexican think-tank said on Tuesday.

"Contractual earnings will increase by 19 percent on average in 1997, but even so real wages will still be far below their level before the crisis," the Private Sector Centre for Economic Studies (CEESP) said.
"As a consquence, growth in private consumption will be just 3.2 percent," the report added.
A fumbled devaluation of the peso in December 1994 plunged the Mexican economy into its worst recession for several decades in 1995, from which it has yet to fully recover.
The CEESP report predicted that although inflation was falling, it would still be 17.4 percent for 1997, compared to a government estimate of 15 percent.

Whereas the export sector had played a vital part in bringing about economic recovery, the report said an increase in both public and private consumption would be needed to ensure the CEESP's growth target of 4.8 percent for the year.
Elsewhere on the macroeconomic front, the CEESP forecast that Mexico would post a trade surplus of $3.279 billion, down on 1996 figures of $6.531 billion, due to imports growing faster than exports.
The report predicted Mexico would chalk up a current account deficit of $5 billion in 1997, up from a 1996 total of 1.76 billion, and compared to a government projection of $4.3 billion.
The peso was seen devaluing by nine percent to close the year at 8.60 per dollar, while bellwether interest rates on 28-day Cetes were expected to average 21 percent in 1997.
